SoCal artist says Trump administration used her fan art: 'I did not and would never consent'

Devin Elle Kurtz soon took to social media saying: “I did not and would never consent to this administration running my fanart through AI and posting it.”

Actual Article Body:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search.   Set us as preferred

Devin Elle Kurtz makes her opinion on generative AI known. For the last few years, the 29-year-old Pasadena artist says she’s been frustrated when strangers tell her that her art style looks AI-generated.

They have it backward, she insists. Kurtz, who has been sharing her art on the internet since she was a teenager, suspects that her viral art may have been used to train AI models. Her Instagram bio reads, “NO AI,” alongside a circle-backslash emoji.

Her feelings on the subject made what she discovered Thursday morning all the more painful, the artist said. Kurtz woke up to multiple emails from fans telling her that the Trump administration’s Department of Education had posted a meme on X that looked eerily similar to one of her works — fan art inspired by one of her favorite scenes from the animated series “Avatar: The Last Airbender.” In the work, Aang and Zuko are shown practicing fire-bending moves as two dragons move around them.

There’s Magic in Learning 🪄 https://t.co/hJdp0Y2qho

The Department of Education’s post includes an image of the two characters in seemingly identical stances, outfits and color scheme. “There’s magic in learning,” reads text added over the image. “Make education great again.”

The Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Thursday.

Kurtz soon took to social media to condemn the Trump administration. She wrote on the platform: “I did not and would never consent to this administration running my fanart through AI and posting it. Can’t even believe I’m saying these words.” Her response had 150,000 likes as of late Thursday night.

“It definitely made me angry,” Kurtz told The Times on Thursday. “Seeing something that I made appropriated with a Make America Great Again-adjacent slogan on it made me quite upset. I knew I wanted to make it really clear that this was not something that I co-signed.”

Kurtz said she made the artwork in 2023 to share her love of the series with its creators and with other fans.

“Fandom at its core is supposed to be humans loving something together,” Kurtz said. “I want to live in a world where the things that I see around me are made by people. That is what being a human being is all about. Not just output for the sake of output.”

Kurtz said several tells led her to conclude that AI was likely used to alter her work. In the version shared by the Trump administration, the dragons have been removed, and the platform the duo is standing on has oddly sized bricks.

Since her fan art is based on existing intellectual property, she doesn’t intend to pursue legal action.

“It would be fantastic if the government didn’t take artists’ work and run it through AI and post it,” Kurtz said.

Kurtz joins a laundry list of artists who have accused the Trump administration of using their work without their knowledge, including singer Olivia Rodrigo and Japanese artist Hiroshi Nagai.

In December, singer Sabrina Carpenter was angered when her song “Juno” was used in the soundtrack for a Department of Homeland Security promotional video featuring clips of officers tackling and handcuffing people.

“[T]his video is evil and disgusting,” Carpenter replied. “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.” The Department of Homeland Security has since deleted that video.

President Trump reshuffles schedule, adds back Iowa and Kansas rallies ahead of midterms

As early voting surges across the country, President Donald Trump is reshuffling his weekend schedule.

Actual Article Body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — As early voting surges across the country, President Donald Trump is reshuffling his weekend schedule to rally Republicans in two states with critical Senate races, underscoring his party’s push to drive turnout ahead of Election Day.

The Republican president will now visit Iowa and Kansas for back-to-back campaign rallies on Sunday, according to a person familiar with his plans who insisted on anonymity to discuss his schedule. Both rallies had previously been canceled.

The last-minute reversal comes amid a nationwide surge in early voting. Nearly 10 million more Americans had cast ballots five days before Election Day than at the same point in 2022, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data. The increases have been particularly pronounced in states with competitive Senate races, including Iowa and Kansas, where early voting is up roughly 30%.

Democrats and Republicans each hope that rise favors them as they fight for control of Congress in an election that has turned largely on affordability issues and the president’s unpopularity. At the start of the month, Trump promised a marathon sprint of his signature rallies to shore up Republican candidates, and he has headlined 25 of them so far in October.

The president on Thursday furiously pushed back at the notion that the initial cancellation of his Kansas rally, which became public as he was returning to Washington from another campaign event in South Carolina, was tied to fatigue or his health. He lashed out at a reporter who asked about the change in his plans for Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is seeking reelection.

“I’m not going to Kansas because he’s doing very well,” Trump said, seeming to refer to Marshall. The president added that “I feel perfect” and that “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas.”

The Republican National Committee initially said in canceling the rallies that Trump would do telerallies instead to reach more voters. But the person familiar with the latest plans said the Iowa and Kansas rallies have been rearranged to accommodate the new telerallies added to Trump’s schedule.

Trump’s original plans had him in Salina, Kansas, on Saturday and in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Then the plans shifted so he would instead do a “72-hour sprint” of phone rallies, meant so the president could reach more voters nationwide, according to the RNC.

Sunday’s rally in Iowa will now be held in Cedar Rapids instead of Dubuque, according to another person familiar with the plans who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share information that was not yet public.

Both Kansas and Iowa are home to battleground Senate races that will help determine whether Republicans hold onto their narrow majority in the chamber in the midterm elections.

Trump has already traveled to both states this month to boost Marshall in Kansas and Republican Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who currently serves in the House.

In an interview with a Kansas City radio station on Friday, Trump called Marshall “fantastic” and credited the senator for pushing his administration on policies benefiting Kansas farmers such as expanding tax-free use of red-dyed diesel.

Trump criticized Marshall’s Democratic challenger, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, as a “radical” who has “caused turmoil with the church because he’s so liberal.” Hamilton has said that if Jesus were standing before them now, “Roger Marshall would call him ‘woke.’”

Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance.

In Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor’s races, more than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50% increase.

Advance voting has also increased more than 30% from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races. In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83%.

Historic amounts of money have flowed into this year’s midterm elections. Republicans have expressed concerns about their voters not turning out amid voter dissatisfaction with Trump and high costs, issues Democrats have focused on in their campaigns.

Michigan Democrats hoped to put a bruising Senate primary behind them after progressive Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in August.

They’ve had no such luck as Election Day approaches.

Stevens reemerged in the final week before the general election, appearing on CNN to reaffirm that she would vote for El-Sayed while calling on him to repair relations with Jewish and Black voters. Her appearance came hours after her fiance said he would vote for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

Then on Friday, after agreeing to campaign alongside El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina in Detroit on Sunday, Stevens released a lengthy statement on social media criticizing her former rival once again. She called on him to condemn an advertisement linking U.S. support for Israel to rising grocery prices and address concerns about his past rhetoric.

“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”

El-Sayed has apologized for some of his past comments while attempting to unify Democrats.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced Thursday that it has revoked or terminated the immigration status of about 2.2 million illegals since President Donald Trump came into office, setting them up for removal from the United States. In doing so, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) ended categorical parole programs, which the Biden administration […]

Actual Article Body:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced Thursday that it has revoked or terminated the immigration status of about 2.2 million illegals since President Donald Trump came into office, setting them up for removal from the United States.

In doing so, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) ended categorical parole programs, which the Biden administration used to offer blanket legal status to millions of migrants who otherwise would have been illegal border crossers. The Trump administration also reformed Temporary Protected Status (TPS), infamously abused by successive American governments to keep foreign populations of Somalians, Haitians, and others in the country in perpetuity, so that it is “once again truly temporary.”

“Those who abuse or flagrantly disregard our immigration system are now on notice that these violations of law will not be tolerated or overlooked,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. “Securing our border was only the beginning. We are restoring integrity to the entire immigration system and putting the safety of our American citizens first.”

DHS announced Friday morning that it had rounded up 4,170 illegal aliens in an 11-day operation in Texas, ostensibly all of whom will be removed from the country.

USCIS is responsible for reviewing and issuing work permits, green cards, and other types of statuses that allow foreigners to legally stay in the country for a period of time. During the Biden administration, this review was essentially turned into one of the final steps in an international human trafficking operation to bring as many illegals into the country as possible and make them legally untouchable.

The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) did the same thing in its Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), as The Federalist reported. Current ORR Senior Advisor John Fabbricatore said that under the Biden administration that office acted as the endpoint of a “smuggling operation” in which nearly half a million Unaccompanied Alien Children (UAC) went missing.

Other USCIS enforcement actions announced Thursday include “denying applications to extend or change nonimmigrant status when no legal basis exists; issuing Notices to Appear to place removable aliens into removal proceedings before an immigration judge; [and] ending the automatic extension of employment authorization documents, ensuring every alien is properly screened and vetted before any work authorization is renewed.”

About 900,000 illegals given legal status under the Biden administration used a now-defunct “CBP One” app, which the Trump administration used to conduct a mass revocation of status. An Obama-appointed federal judge in Boston stopped the move for now, but the app has been revamped as “CBP Home,” and is used to facilitate the return of foreigners to the proper countries.

While the Trump administration virtually ended all illegal border crossings, it also cut legal immigration in half. The State Department was issuing about 52,000 visas a month prior to Trump’s second stint in the White House.

Other USCIS enforcement actions announced Thursday include “denying applications to extend or change nonimmigrant status when no legal basis exists; issuing Notices to Appear to place removable aliens into removal proceedings before an immigration judge; [and] ending the automatic extension of employment authorization documents, ensuring every alien is properly screened and vetted before any work authorization is renewed.”

About 900,000 illegals given legal status under the Biden administration used a now-defunct “CBP One” app, which the Trump administration used to conduct a mass revocation of status. An Obama-appointed federal judge in Boston stopped the move for now, but the app has been revamped as “CBP Home,” and is used to facilitate the return of foreigners to the proper countries.

While the Trump administration virtually ended all illegal border crossings, it also cut legal immigration in half. The State Department was issuing about 52,000 visas a month prior to Trump’s second stint in the White House.
